cards.front: What is the main job of meiosis, and why does it matter?
cards.back: Meiosis makes cells with **half** the starting chromosome number, such as eggs and sperm. Fusing an egg and sperm restores the full number.
cards.hint: Think about what happens when an egg and sperm fuse.

cards.front: What does meiosis I separate, and how does that halve the chromosome number?
cards.back: Meiosis I separates **homologous chromosomes**, so each cell gets one chromosome from each pair. Each cell then has half the original number.
cards.hint: Which pair is pulled apart in anaphase I?

cards.front: How does the first division of meiosis differ from mitosis?
cards.back: Meiosis I separates **homologous chromosomes**, while mitosis separates sister chromatids. Meiosis also pairs homologs before they separate.
cards.hint: Compare what is pulled apart in each first division.

cards.front: What are germ cells, and where are they found in humans?
cards.back: **Germ cells** are cells in reproductive organs that give rise to eggs or sperm. In humans they are in the ovaries and testes.
cards.hint: Think about what the cells eventually become.

cards.back: A **homologous pair** is two chromosomes carrying the same genes, with one inherited from each parent. Their versions of the genes may differ.

cards.front: What happens during meiosis I, in stage order?
cards.back: Prophase I: homologs pair and can exchange DNA. Metaphase I: pairs line up at the middle. Anaphase I: homologs move to opposite poles. Telophase I and cytokinesis: two cells form.
cards.hint: Start with the stage where homologs pair.

cards.front: What happens during meiosis II, and what is the usual outcome?
cards.back: Chromosomes line up individually, then **sister chromatids** separate in anaphase II. Cytokinesis then divides each cell, usually giving four **haploid** cells.
cards.hint: Compare with mitosis: no DNA copying happens first.

cards.front: Common mistake: meiosis I separates sister chromatids. Is this correct?
cards.back: No. Meiosis I separates **homologous chromosomes**, which reduces the chromosome number. Sister chromatids separate later, in anaphase II.

cards.front: Is DNA copied again between meiosis I and meiosis II?
cards.back: No. DNA is copied **once**, before meiosis I. There is no second round of copying before meiosis II, which is why the number is halved.
cards.hint: Count how many times DNA is copied.

cards.front: A human body cell has 46 chromosomes. How many chromosomes does an egg or sperm have?
cards.back: **23** chromosomes. Meiosis produces haploid cells with one set of chromosomes, so the number is halved from 46.
A **haploid** cell has one set of chromosomes. A diploid cell has two sets.

cards.front: Why are cells from meiosis genetically different, while mitotic daughter cells are usually alike?
cards.back: Meiosis pairs homologs and can exchange matching DNA segments, so the cells can differ. Mitosis does not normally pair homologs, so daughter cells are usually genetically alike.
cards.hint: Think about pairing and DNA exchange.

cards.front: What is mitosis for, and what does it usually produce?
cards.back: Mitosis supports **growth**, tissue repair, and cell replacement. It has one division and usually makes two cells that keep the starting chromosome number.
